issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a class named 'Stock' (and show SealSaloon.stock typed as Stock), but the template repository provides an 'Inventory' class that implements the expected stock methods while Stock.java is empty. The solution also uses Inventory as the shared stock. This name/type mismatch between 'Stock' (in the specification/UML) and 'Inventory' (in the template/solution) is a structural inconsistency that can confuse students about which class they must implement or use for the shared stock attribute.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the naming consistent across specification and code. Either (a) rename the provided Inventory class to Stock in the template (and update references in tests/solution/sample code), or (b) update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock, and clarify that students should use the provided Inventory class as the shared stock. Alternatively, provide a simple Stock wrapper that delegates to Inventory and include it in the template so the UML and code match.

issues.description: The problem statement (UML and text) refers to a class named 'Stock' as the shared saloon inventory, but the provided template and the reference solution implement this functionality in a class named 'Inventory' (Inventory.java) while Stock.java is empty. This mismatch forces students to look for inventory methods in Stock.java (as described in the spec) and not find them, creating a mapping barrier between the specification and the codebase.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the naming consistent: either (A) rename the Inventory class to Stock (move/merge Inventory.java implementation into Stock.java and update all references in SealSaloon and other files), or (B) update the problem statement and UML to refer to 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock'. Prefer option A (rename Inventory -> Stock) to match the exercise description and UML while keeping method names and behavior unchanged.
